name: Low Desert Loop — the long way
subtitle: Death Valley · Palm Springs · Anza-Borrego · Joshua Tree · Route 66 · Valley of Fire
summary: A warm loop out of Las Vegas that never climbs into the cold. Death Valley first, then Route 66 across the Mojave, the Coachella Valley, Anza-Borrego, Joshua Tree, the old road east through Needles and Kingman, and a finish on the red rock at Valley of Fire rather than in an airport car park. Nothing sleeps above 2,600 feet, no night is expected to freeze, and five of the fourteen days involve no driving between towns.
startEnd: Las Vegas, NV (Harry Reid International — LAS)

mustSee.name: Zabriskie Point
mustSee.why: Golden badlands at sunset, ten minutes from where you sleep. The best view in Death Valley for the least effort.

mustSee.name: Badwater Basin
mustSee.why: The lowest point in North America, 282 ft below sea level, at 18°C in January. Walk out onto the salt flats.

mustSee.name: Mesquite Flat Dunes
mustSee.why: Go at sunrise. Dunes the kids can run down, before the wind picks up and the light goes flat.

mustSee.name: Elmer's Bottle Tree Ranch
mustSee.why: Free, on the old Route 66 alignment, and unlike anything else on either version. Ten minutes, and worth the detour.

mustSee.name: Palm Springs Aerial Tramway
mustSee.why: Ten minutes from the valley floor to 8,500 feet. The only snow anyone will see on this trip, and you choose whether to go up to it.

mustSee.name: Galleta Meadows
mustSee.why: A 350-foot steel serpent crossing a road in the desert, and 129 other sculptures. Free, and the best surprise on the route.

mustSee.name: The Slot
mustSee.why: A slot canyon you walk yourself, with no permit and no guide. The Southwest Loop pays about $580 for six to do this at Antelope.

mustSee.name: Cholla Cactus Garden
mustSee.why: Ten acres of teddy-bear cholla lit from behind at the end of the day. A quarter-mile loop, and the best photograph in Joshua Tree.

mustSee.name: Skull Rock
mustSee.why: Right beside the road, and the one every child on this trip will want a photograph of.

mustSee.name: Roy's Motel, Route 66
mustSee.why: One neon sign in an abandoned town in the middle of the Mojave. This is the one the kids will talk about.

mustSee.name: The Fire Wave
mustSee.why: Striped red and white sandstone at the end of a short flat walk, on the last full day. A better finish than a car park near the airport.

watchOuts.title: Book Palm Springs first, then Borrego
watchOuts.text: Book Palm Springs first, then Borrego Springs, then Valley of Fire if you are camping. January is high season in the Coachella Valley — the exact opposite of the Southwest Loop, where the cold made everything cheap. Death Valley, Barstow and Needles have far more slack.

watchOuts.title: It is warm, not hot
watchOuts.text: No night on this route is expected to freeze. The coolest stops are Barstow, Twentynine Palms and Boulder City, all around 2,000 to 2,500 feet, where January lows average 3 or 4°C. A cold snap can put any of them a degree below for a few hours before dawn, so pack for 2°C nights — but there is no sustained freeze anywhere, and nothing here needs winterising.

watchOuts.title: Needles is warm, not smart
watchOuts.text: Needles is a small, faded railroad town and the lodging is basic motels rather than anything with a lobby. It is on the route because it sits at 495 feet on the Colorado, which makes it the warmest bed of the trip, and because it is genuinely on Route 66. If the party would rather have a proper room, Lake Havasu is 42 miles south — warmer weather is not the reason to go there, comfort is.

watchOuts.title: Font's Point is a four-wheel-drive road
watchOuts.text: The road to Font's Point is four miles of soft sand off the Borrego Salton Seaway. It needs four-wheel drive and it strands two-wheel-drive vehicles regularly. A minivan will not make it. Either rent something suitable for the day, take a local jeep tour, or accept that this one is off the list.

watchOuts.title: There is no hotel inside Valley of Fire
watchOuts.text: There is no hotel inside Valley of Fire. The park has two campgrounds — Atlatl Rock has hookups, Arch Rock does not — and both are reservation-only. In a car, the nearest rooms are in Overton about fifteen minutes away. This is the one stop where the motorhome build has the better night.

watchOuts.title: Death Valley is still closing roads
watchOuts.text: Flood damage persists. Bonnie Clare Road and Scotty's Castle are closed with no reopening date, North Highway has loose gravel and missing shoulders, southern Badwater Road has soft shoulders and unpaved sections, and Emigrant Campground is closed indefinitely. Check the park's conditions page a week before departure.

watchOuts.title: Long empty stretches — fill up early
watchOuts.text: California fuel runs well above Nevada and Arizona. Fill up in Nevada before you drive in, top off in Barstow rather than inside Death Valley, where in-park fuel at Furnace Creek is notably expensive, and fill again in Arizona on the way home. The Amboy stretch of Route 66 has no fuel at all for about eighty miles.

watchOuts.title: The park pass does not cover the state parks
watchOuts.text: The America the Beautiful pass covers Death Valley and Joshua Tree. It does not cover Anza-Borrego or the Salton Sea, which are California state parks, or Valley of Fire, which is a Nevada state park. None of them are expensive; they are just not free.

watchOuts.title: The Oatman Highway is not for everybody
watchOuts.text: The Oatman Highway over Sitgreaves Pass is steep with blind hairpins, and most rental agreements effectively prohibit it. It is passable but tight in a car and out of the question in a motorhome. The I-40 route through Kingman is the one in the plan, and it is ten miles longer but half an hour faster.

pros: No night is expected to freeze. Nothing on this route sleeps above 2,600 feet.
Two national parks, four state parks and 200 miles of original Route 66, out and back from a single airport.
Short days: 100 miles a day on average, and five of the fourteen involve no driving between towns.
It finishes on the red rock at Valley of Fire rather than in a car park near the airport, and the last day is a 63-mile run to the plane.
January is the best month of the year to be in the low desert. Palm Springs runs to 21 or 22°C and Death Valley to around 18°C.
The motorhome stops being a compromise. Its worst problem on the Southwest Loop was seven freezing nights, and this route does not have one.
cons: Two national parks instead of five. The warm places are the low places, and the famous parks are nearly all high.
January is high season in the Coachella Valley, so Palm Springs is the one expensive stop — the reverse of the Southwest Loop, where the cold made everything cheap.
Day 4 is 177 miles of mostly empty desert between Death Valley and Route 66. It is the longest day on the route.
Font's Point needs four-wheel drive — four miles of soft sand. Neither build reaches it.
Needles is a faded railroad town and the lodging is basic motels. It is on the route because it is warm and on Route 66, not because it is comfortable.
Death Valley still has flood damage: Scotty’s Castle and Bonnie Clare Road are closed indefinitely, and several roads have soft shoulders and unpaved sections.

notConsidered.reason: A 110-mile round trip from Furnace Creek for a single crater. It fits when Death Valley gets four nights, not three.

Santa Monica Pier is the western end of Route 66, and it slots between Barstow and Palm Springs for only 125 extra miles — genuinely cheap, and it would let the route run Route 66 from the Pacific to Arizona. Left out because the point of this trip is empty desert, and January is the wettest month of LA's year.

The better Route 66 town and the better rooms, but it sits at 3,366 feet and averages a January low of 0°C. It would be the one freezing night on a route built to avoid them. You drive through it and stop at the Powerhouse instead.

Warm, comfortable, and 42 miles off the Route 66 line. It is a lake town with a novelty bridge rather than anything to do with the road, and in January it is too cold to swim. It gets two nights on the Sonoran Loop instead.

notConsidered.place: Zion, Bryce and the Grand Canyon
notConsidered.reason: The famous parks on the Southwest Loop sit between 4,000 and 8,000 feet. Warm and high do not go together in January — that is the entire reason this route exists.
5,200 feet, freezing at night in January, and on the wrong side of the map. It belongs to the Southwest Loop.
Warmer still, and the giant saguaro grows nowhere on this route. But reaching Tucson from Las Vegas costs you a 288-mile day. That trip is the Sonoran Loop.
No hookups, no potable water, no cell service, and the York Fire burned close to 100,000 acres in 2023 including much of the Cima Dome Joshua tree forest.

Genuinely remarkable, and only twenty minutes past the south end of the Salton Sea — but routing the day through it costs 76 extra miles and two extra hours. It sits on the far shore from the road you are on.
Trailer rentals do not include a tow vehicle, and the major rental companies prohibit towing outright. Turo treats towing as a prohibited use that voids damage protection.

moneySavers.detail: Day use is $10 at the visitor centre and campground, and The Slot, Font's Point and every roadside trailhead are free. The Southwest Loop's equivalent — a guided slot canyon at Antelope — runs about $580 for six.
A hundred and thirty life-size metal sculptures — sloths, raptors, horses and a 350-foot serpent — scattered across open land around Borrego Springs. No gate, no ticket, no opening hours.

moneySavers.item: Twentynine Palms instead of inside Joshua Tree
moneySavers.detail: The park's own campgrounds have no hookups, no dump and mostly no water. A full-hookup site in town costs about the same as a dry site inside and you can shower — and you are ten minutes from the north entrance either way.
Buy bedding and kitchen gear at a Las Vegas store on day one for $200-300 and leave it behind. Cheaper than per-person kit fees for six.

moneySavers.item: Go midweek in the Coachella Valley
moneySavers.detail: January is peak season in Palm Springs and the weekend premium is steep. Arriving Sunday or Monday rather than Friday is the single biggest lever in the lodging line.

Covers Death Valley and Joshua Tree — both national parks on this route. It does NOT cover Anza-Borrego or the Salton Sea, which are California state parks, or Valley of Fire, which is a Nevada state park.

options.name: Motorhome
options.tagline: Cheapest, simplest, and no longer the cold one
options.summary: Transport and lodging in one vehicle, so there is nothing to book at every stop and you cook instead of eating out. On the Southwest Loop the catch was seven freezing nights; here there are none.

vehicle.detail: Cruise America C30 · sleeps 7 · 7 seatbelts · 30 ft long, 8.33 ft wide, 12.2 ft high
vehicle.notes: Book by seatbelt count, not sleeping capacity. On this route there is no reason to take the smaller C25 for clearance — the only length limit you meet is Death Valley's 25 ft on Artist's Drive and Dante's View, and a C25 measures 24.93 ft, which is a three-inch margin you should not rely on.

2.label: Not in the motorhome:
2.text: Artist's Drive is closed to vehicles over 25 ft. Take the separate rental car — it is in the budget for exactly this.

3.label: Not in the motorhome:
3.text: The final climb to Dante's View has the same 25 ft limit. Rental car again. These two are the only places in Death Valley the motorhome cannot go.

7.label: Not in the motorhome:
7.text: Font's Point — four miles of soft sand off the Borrego Salton Seaway. Nothing without four-wheel drive gets there, so this one is out for the car build too.

8.label: You sleep in town, not in the park.
8.text: Joshua Tree's own campgrounds cap at around 25 to 35 ft and have no hookups, no dump station and mostly no water. A full-hookup site in Twentynine Palms costs about the same and you are ten minutes from the north entrance.

11.label: Not in the motorhome:
11.text: The Oatman Highway over Sitgreaves Pass — steep, blind hairpins, no room for a 30-footer. The map shows the I-40 route through Kingman, which is ten miles longer and half an hour faster.

12.label: The one night you have the better bed:
12.text: There is no hotel inside Valley of Fire. Atlatl Rock campground has hookups and puts you in the park for sunrise on the sandstone. Reserve it — all sites are reservation-only.

options.name: Car and lodging
options.tagline: More expensive, more comfortable, and it unlocks the Oatman Highway
options.summary: A seven-seater and a room every night. It costs meaningfully more, and almost all of the gap is food and lodging — but on this route it buys comfort rather than warmth, because the motorhome is not cold here either.

vehicle.detail: Chrysler Pacifica · Honda Odyssey · Chevrolet Suburban · 7 seats
vehicle.notes: A minivan is better for people, a Suburban better for luggage. From Las Vegas, including airport concession fees. Neither will get you to Font's Point — that needs four-wheel drive.

Real beds, and rooms you can spread six people across

2.label: Open to you:
2.text: Artist's Drive, with no second rental car needed.

3.label: Open to you:
3.text: The climb to Dante's View, 5,450 ft up over Badwater.

7.label: Still not open to you:
7.text: Font's Point needs four-wheel drive — four miles of soft sand, and it strands two-wheel-drive vehicles regularly. A minivan will not make it. This is the one place on the route neither build reaches without renting something else for the day.

11.label: Open to you:
11.text: The Oatman Highway. Ten miles shorter than the interstate and half an hour slower, because it is a mountain pass with hairpins — and the wild burros come to the car window. Check the rental agreement first; many effectively prohibit Sitgreaves Pass. The map shows the detour.

12.label: No rooms in the park.
12.text: Valley of Fire has campgrounds and nothing else. The nearest rooms are in Overton, about fifteen minutes from the east entrance — which means driving back in for sunrise if you want it.

days.headline: Below sea level by lunchtime
days.notes: Pick up the vehicle and drive straight in. Furnace Creek sits 190 feet below sea level and is the warmest place you will sleep all trip — January highs around 18°C, lows around 4°C.

days.headline: Out of the valley and onto Route 66
days.notes: The one leg that looks dull on the map, and is not. You leave Death Valley by the southern road, cross the Mojave and land on the original alignment of Route 66. Calico is a silver town that went bust in 1896 and was rebuilt as a park — kitsch, and the kids will love it.

pois.name: Calico Ghost Town
pois.caption: A silver town that went bust in 1896, rebuilt as a park.

photos.caption: A silver town that went bust in 1896, rebuilt as a park.

days.headline: Into the warmest air on the trip
days.notes: Start on the old road for Elmer's Bottle Tree Ranch — a forest of welded steel trees hung with thousands of glass bottles, free, and unlike anything else on either version. Then over the pass into the Coachella Valley, which runs to 21 or 22°C in January. One night here, so the tramway is this afternoon.

days.headline: A palm oasis, then down the Salton Sea
days.notes: Indian Canyons first thing — Agua Caliente land, a real palm oasis in a desert canyon, and a walk that suits everyone. Then south along the west shore of the Salton Sea, a lake 230 feet below sea level that exists only because an irrigation canal broke in 1905 and took two years to close.

days.headline: Six hundred thousand acres of state park
days.notes: Borrego Palm Canyon is a three-mile round trip to a palm grove and, in a wet year, a waterfall. The Slot is a genuine slot canyon you walk yourself — no permit, no guide, no fee. Font's Point looks out over the Borrego Badlands and is the best view in the park, but the road to it is four miles of soft sand.

days.headline: Up out of the low desert to Joshua Tree
days.notes: You climb about 1,500 feet, and this is the first night that feels properly cool — 3 or 4°C rather than the 8 or 9°C you have had. Come in by the south entrance and the Cholla Cactus Garden is the first thing you meet.

days.headline: A full day in Joshua Tree
days.notes: Two deserts meet inside this park — the low Colorado and the high Mojave — and the Joshua trees only grow on the high side. Nearly everything worth doing is a short walk from a car park, which is exactly what you want on day nine with six people.

days.headline: Amboy Crater and the empty Route 66
days.notes: North on Amboy Road onto the loneliest surviving stretch of Route 66. Amboy Crater is a 250-foot cinder cone you can walk into. Roy's Motel is one neon sign in an empty town and it is the photograph everybody takes. Needles sits at 495 feet on the Colorado — the warmest bed on the route.

days.headline: Kingman, the burros and the dam
days.notes: East into Arizona for Kingman, where Route 66 crosses US-93 and the Powerhouse museum sits inside a 1907 power station. Then north to Hoover Dam and Boulder City, built in 1931 to house the men who constructed it and still the only town in Nevada where gambling is illegal. In a car you can take the Oatman Highway instead — ten miles shorter and half an hour slower, because it is a mountain pass with hairpins.

days.headline: Back to the red rock
days.notes: A short morning drive that puts you inside Nevada's oldest state park with the whole afternoon left. Bright red Aztec sandstone, petroglyphs up a steel staircase at Atlatl Rock, and short walks that suit kids. All campsites are reservation-only, and there is no hotel inside the park.

days.headline: The last full day, and the best rock on the route
days.notes: The Fire Wave is striped red and white sandstone at the end of a short flat walk. White Domes adds a slot canyon and the remains of a 1960s film set. Elephant Rock is ten minutes from the east entrance. A better last day than a car park near the airport.

days.headline: An hour and a half to the plane
days.notes: Sixty-three miles to the airport, so there is time for one more walk before you go. Allow half a day for the vehicle return process.
